newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers meet on Italy as EMU questions remain.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers meet on Italy as EMU questions remain.

text.p: European Union finance ministers met on Monday to discuss Italy's plans for qualifying for the single currency as the whole EMU project appeared to be pulled in different directions.
The ministers, in their first meeting under the Luxembourg EU presidency, were set to consider Italy's covergence plan, its road map to economic and monetary union (EMU).
"The Italian convergence programme very clearly shows that Italy is moving in a good direction," Luxembourg's Jean-Claude Juncker told reporters as he arrived for the meeting.
But Juncker, who is both finance minister and prime minister of the Grand Duchy, said Rome needed to do more to get its economy in line with others.
"We have to encourage them to take further steps," he said.

Italy's hopes of joining the single currency in 1999, once considered slim, have been bolstered recently by growing expectations that the entry criteria for the euro will be applied in a flexible manner.
This stems in the main from the attitude of the French government, which admits that it is unlikely to meet the criteria for EMU this year but says the project will go ahead on time anyway.
Talk of a flexible approach to EMU, however, has put intense pressure on Germany, which is having its own difficulties meeting the criteria but which is the bastion of fiscal rigour.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl was forced by domestic political pressure last week to pledge that there would be no loosening of the criteria.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, meanwhile, takes part in Monday's ministerial meeting while a member of his own party at home openly discusses putting off EMU.

Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber told the Financial Times in an interview: "A controlled delay would certainly be better than a weak European currency. It would mean holding to the goal of the euro and holding firm to the criteria."
In this way, EMU could perhaps start "on January 1, 2000 or 2001," the newspaper quoted him as saying. Under the current formula, EMU is due to start on January 1, 1999.

The Italian blueprint to be studied by the ministers foresees a budget deficit of 3.0 percent of Gross Domestic Product this year, in line with the criterion for EMU. It predicts the ratio will drop to 2.8 percent in 1998.
In terms of growth, GDP is expected to rise 1.2 percent this year and 2.0 percent in 1998.
The ministers are expected, however, to tell Italy that it needs to do more to curb spending, particularly on pensions, if it is to reach these goals.
